slides.heading: Ellipsis
bullets: Ellipsis is the leaving out of one or more words that are understood.
The missing words are still “there” in meaning — we just don’t say them.
In a command, the subject you is understood:  “[You] shut the door.”
In a comparison, a verb is often left out:  “He is older than I [am].”

slides.heading: Practice — Supply the Missing Word
slides.instruction: What word is understood (left out) in each sentence?

slides.heading: Simple & Complete Subject
bullets: “Subject” still names the notion the proposition is about (Lesson 1); “simple” and “complete” only say how much of the wording we point to.
The Simple Subject is the single word that names it, without modifiers.
The Complete Subject is that word together with all its modifiers.
“A great storm is raging.” — simple subject: storm; complete subject: a great storm.
Find the simple subject by asking who or what the proposition is about.

slides.heading: Practice — Name the Simple Subject
slides.instruction: Name the simple subject — the single word, without modifiers.

slides.heading: Simple & Complete Predicate
bullets: The Simple Predicate is the bare verb, without modifiers; the Complete Predicate is that verb with all its modifiers.
“The storm rages furiously.” — simple predicate: rages; complete predicate: rages furiously.
With a copula (is/are) the verb only asserts — the predicate is the word affirmed:  “Iron is heavy” → predicate heavy, copula is.
Find the simple predicate by asking what the subject does or is.

slides.heading: Practice — Name the Simple Predicate
slides.instruction: Name the simple predicate — the bare verb, without modifiers.

slides.heading: Abridgment
bullets: A complex sentence can be shortened — abridged — into a simple one.
Turn a subordinate clause into a phrase or a single word.
“I knew that it was he.” → “I knew it to be him.”
“Because the weather was bad, the fair was not held.” → “The weather being bad, the fair was not held.”

items: In “Shut the door,” what subject is understood?
answers: The leaving out of words that are understood.
The single word that names the subject, without modifiers.
The subject with all its modifiers.
Shortening a complex sentence by turning a clause into a phrase or word.
